notes.1: This was a fairly straightforward question where most candidates were able to choose some of the correct statements referring to backing storage. The main confusion was between ROM and RAM. A few candidates were able to achieve full marks, with most candidates achieving approximately three of the four marks.
notes.2: Almost every candidate correctly identified Website designers. Some were able to correctly include Delivery drivers. Incorrect answers appeared to have been chosen at random. Most candidates were able to achieve one correct answer in this question.
notes.3: This question needed to be read in full before starting on the answer. The question related to an emergency situation where the senders needed to be rescued. However, some candidates thought this system was an answering service rather than an emergency situation. Some answers related to reading the text message at a later date or including videos. Some thought that texts could be sent if there was no signal rather than a weaker signal. Answers that indicated that text would not require more than the minimum mobile connection to work, achieved a mark.
notes.4: This question was well answered by most candidates with many achieving three of the four marks. Many candidates were able to achieve full marks by correctly identifying which statement more likely would be addressed by interviews, observation or questionnaires.
notes.5: On the whole this question was well answered by most candidates.
notes.7: Many candidates showed some understanding of the issues but did not give enough detail in their answers. However, many candidates were able to attempt answers for much of the question.
notes.8: The question asked for features used in a spreadsheet and then how it could be used to monitor the progress of candidates. As with previous answers, candidates need to expand on their answers and not to write vague answers. It was clear than many candidates understood the features but could not explain fully how they could be used. A popular correct answer was the use of graphs and conditional formatting, but they were often not linked to any meaningful monitoring of the candidate.
notes.9: This style of question had been set previously and looks at candidates use of email. Candidates needed to evaluate their own use of email rather than a general use of email. Candidates need to evaluate strategies the use and a reason; many candidates were able to explain a strategy but not a reason for its use. Some reasonable answers were seen but candidates should beware of ‘light’ answers. ‘I never put personal details in an email’ is wrong. ‘I never put personal details in an email to someone I do not know’ is right.
notes.10: Most candidates were able to produce an answer for most parts of the question.
notes.11: A few candidates appear to have misread the question and thought they were being asking about analysis of the website rather than the needs of the audience. The question required the needs of the mature candidates to be analysed in relation to a new website. As with other questions in this paper many candidates lacked depth in their answer giving loose statements without expansion or reasoning. If colours, fonts etc. are described then the reason for the colours, sizes, types must be given for marks to be awarded. Most candidates described what should be included in the web site not the needs of the candidates. A few candidates gave answers relating to the relevance of the content/balance of images and text/easy to navigate. Some referred to the use of videos/picture but did not specify as to what information they would provide e.g. events, sport activities.
notes.12: On the whole most of this question was well answered with many candidates achieving at least half of the available marks. Many candidates did well on parts (a) and (b) but less so on part (c) .
notes.13: On the whole most candidates were able to achieve at least half of the available marks with the question. Candidates appeared to have an understand of what a hyperlink was and how to set up a bookmark but did not do as well on explaining what an anchor was.
notes.14: This question was misread by some candidates who mixed up magnetic tape with magnetic stripes from credit cards. The question asked for the advantages and disadvantages of magnetic tape over flash memory. Answers therefore had to be comparative. For example, ‘Data access time is slow’ is not enough. To achieve a mark a candidate should write ‘Data access time is slower’. As with other question there was a lack of detail i.e. magnetic tape is slower without explanation. Some candidates achieved general marks for stating magnetic tapes were larger and therefore not as easily lost. It did become apparent that many candidates did not understand what magnetic tapes were.
notes.15: There was some understanding in that the streaming did not result in the copy being downloaded and therefore taking up storage space and that you had to be connected to the internet. Those that understood the concept of legal streaming were able to achieve marks here. Very few gave advantages and disadvantages. INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY
notes.5a: Almost every candidate successfully chose ‘web browser’ as the software most likely to be used to display a web page.
notes.5b: Almost every candidate wrote that a personal internet journal was a blog. A few chose other answers including a cookie.
notes.5c: This part of the question was more challenging than parts (a) and (b) . Many candidates knew that a wiki was a web application that could be edited by a group. However, some candidates thought the answer was fax.
notes.6a: This was a straight-forward question, but many candidates missed the sentence in the question that stated that the file name should not include spaces. Every question needs to be read thoroughly before answering it, in order to see all the rules that need to be applied. One or two candidates mistakenly wrote a short descriptive piece which could not achieve credit.
notes.6b: Many candidates were not able to successfully write out the file path for storing the database from Question 6(a) . A few managed to write down the path but got the order of the subdirectories reversed. Some candidates understood the file path but missed off the final slash. A few wrote descriptions instead of giving a file path.
notes.6c: Many candidates appear to have misread the question; some left the answer blank. Some candidates wrote about zipping the file and then sending it rather than explaining why the file would need to be compressed. Some candidates realised that email systems have a limit on the file size that can be transmitted but then struggled to get a second reason like it takes longer to upload/download the file.
notes.7a: Many candidates realised that the default password may be known to others and therefore would need to be changed. Whilst many candidates had the idea that the security of the home network could be at risk and might get hacked.
notes.7b: A few candidates were able to mention data packets, radio waves but not in any coherent way. Mostly a mark was achieved by mentioning the need to enter a password. A few candidates mentioned handshaking but again the answer given was very vague. Many candidates simply wrote that the device was turned on and so was the Wi-Fi.
notes.7c: Many candidates appear not to have read the question in full. The question stated that even if the file size was reduced it could not be sent by email, and that other hardware was not available. However, some candidates stated that the file could be compressed whilst others stated that it could be saved on a pen drive. Brand names are not allowed in the examination answers therefore answers that include brand names cannot achieve credit.
notes.7d: A few candidates stated that encryption could be used, which had already been given in the question. Many candidates were able to mention firewall and anti-virus. Even though strong passwords have been mentioned in numerous mark schemes candidates often forget to describe passwords as such. A few mentioned using a VPN.
notes.10a: Most candidates achieved a couple of marks for this question. However, when candidates read the question fully, they understood that they needed to write down field names. A few candidates did not achieve marks due to inappropriate field names, data examples or for using disallowed symbols or spaces in the field names. A common mistake was to put data types or examples of data, which did not answer the question.
notes.10b: Many candidates achieved at least a mark on this question. Although many examples of this type of practical question have been asked in the past, many candidates were not describing how to do the process just what the process was, to change the field from integer to 2 decimal places. Generally, quite well-answered but with a lack of precision regarding the actions taken. Some candidates struggled to write an answer for this question.
notes.10c: Many candidates only achieved one mark. Mostly, candidates had no idea of the advantages and disadvantages and made vague references to easier/harder to use, use of databases when they meant tables. Some referred to duplication of data but obscurely. As with part (b) come candidates struggled to write an answer for this part of the question.
notes.12a: Most candidates were able to achieve a mark for this part of the question. Most were able to correctly identify ‘crop’ as the editing technique used.
notes.12bi: Most candidates were able to achieve the two marks out of the three. As with other questions this year the depth of answer was lacking.
notes.12bii: Part (ii) was as well answered as part (i) with some good descriptions of how to insert, format and align an image into the document. As candidates appeared to understand the inserting of the image better than creating the columns there was better detail in their answers.
notes.12c: Some candidates did not realise that the branding had to cover the whole of the organisations documents and therefore just wrote about one document. Some candidates mixed up style with spreadsheet styles. Some candidates struggled to produce an answer for this question and therefore this question.
notes.13ai: Candidates appeared to understand what a bookmark was but could not always explain it in enough detail. Too many described a bookmark as ‘saving a website’ or ‘saving a web page’ instead of describing the saving of a link to that website or web page. Some candidates looked at bookmark as a non-IT element and referred to it as in marking where one has got to on a page or in a book.
notes.13aii: The term anchor was not well understood and therefore achieved less marks than other parts of the question. Some made up answers about keeping the page in one place. There were too many no responses in this question. Those that understood the term achieved good marks.
notes.13aiii: This question was well answered by most candidates who clearly understood what a hyperlink was. A large majority of candidates achieved marks for stating it was a link on a word, that when clicked took the user to another website or web page.
notes.13b: Having not understood what a bookmark was it was surprising to see that many candidates could explain how to create one. The process was well understood, and many candidates scored maximum marks.
